title: Earning, Budgeting and Saving
bigQuestion: How can you make the money you earn cover what you need today and still grow for later?

story.title: The Smaller Number
story.kicker: Marcus worked 40 hours and expected one number. The check showed another.
paragraphs: Marcus is fifteen. This summer he got his first job at a snow-cone stand near a Chicago park. The pay was $12 an hour in this example. In two weeks he worked 40 hours. He did the math on the bus: 40 times $12 is $480. He already knew what he would buy.

On Friday his manager handed him an envelope. Inside was a pay stub, a paper that lists what you earned and what was taken out. At the top it said $480. At the bottom, next to the words net pay, it said a smaller number. Marcus stared at it. Had someone made a mistake?

His aunt Rosa looked at the stub with him. She pointed to each line in the middle. One line was Social Security. One was Medicare. One was federal income tax, and one was Illinois income tax. "Nobody made a mistake," she said. "This is the money that pays for roads, schools and help for older people. Everyone who works sees these lines."

Then Rosa asked a question that stuck with him. "Now that you know the real number, what is your plan for it?" Marcus did not have a plan. He had a wish list. By the end of the summer he would learn the difference, and he would watch a small pile of savings start to grow on its own.
story.think: Why do you think the number at the bottom of a pay stub is smaller than the number at the top? Who uses the money that was taken out?

lessons.title: Ways People Earn Income
lessons.mainIdea: Income is money you receive, most often from work, and it comes in several forms.
reading: Think of three workers. Dana earns $15 an hour at a grocery store (an example wage). Luis earns a salary of $52,000 a year. Kim serves food and earns a lower hourly wage plus tips from customers. All three receive *income*, money that comes in.

A *wage* is pay for each hour you work. If Dana works 30 hours, she earns 30 times $15, or $450. A *salary* is a fixed amount for a year, paid in equal parts. Luis is paid every two weeks, 26 times a year, so each check starts at $52,000 divided by 26, or $2,000.

Tips are extra money customers give for good service. Young people also get income from an allowance or small jobs like mowing lawns. Adults may earn interest from savings or money from a business. A common mistake is to think income only means a paycheck. Any money that comes in counts.

words.d: money a person receives, from work, gifts, savings or a business
pay for each hour of work
a set amount of pay for a year of work, paid in equal parts

look.title: Two Summer Jobs
look.text: Job A pays $11 an hour for 20 hours a week. Job B pays a flat $250 a week for the same work. Both are example amounts.
look.prompt: Which job pays more each week? Show your math.

check.q: Dana earns $15 an hour and works 30 hours. What is her pay before anything is taken out?
check.why: Hourly pay times hours: $15 x 30 = $450.

check.q: Which of these is a salary?
choices: $48,000 a year paid in equal parts
check.why: A salary is a fixed yearly amount. The others are a wage, tips and an allowance.

check.q: Luis earns $52,000 a year, paid 26 times a year. How much is each check before taxes?
check.why: $52,000 divided by 26 is $2,000. Dividing by 12 would give a monthly amount, not an every-two-weeks one.

lessons.title: Why Some Jobs Pay More
lessons.mainIdea: Jobs that need rare skills or training, or that few people want to do, usually pay more.
reading: A lifeguard and a nurse both keep people safe. Yet the nurse usually earns more per hour. Why? Wages are a price, the price of work. Like other prices, they depend on how many people can do the job and how many employers want them.

Becoming a nurse takes years of school. Fewer people have that skill, and hospitals need many nurses. Many people can learn lifeguarding in a short course. The skills and knowledge a worker builds are called *human capital*. More human capital usually means higher pay.

Other things matter too. Hard or risky jobs, like work on a high bridge, often pay extra. Jobs in big cities may pay more because living there costs more. A common mistake is to think pay shows how important a job is. It mostly shows how scarce the skill is compared with how many employers want it.

words.d: the skills, knowledge and training a worker has
the place where workers offer their work and employers hire them

look.title: Two Paths
look.text: Jada could start work at 18 at a store. Or she could spend two years training to become an electrician, earning little during training but more after.
look.prompt: What does Jada give up by training? What might she gain later?

check.q: Why do jobs that need long training often pay more?
choices: The government sets every wage by law
Those jobs have more workers than they need
Fewer people have the skills, so employers compete for them
check.why: Pay is a price for work. Scarce skills that employers want earn a higher price.

check.q: Which is an example of building human capital?
check.why: Human capital is skill and knowledge. A class builds skill.

check.q: A job is dangerous and few people want it. What usually happens to its pay?
choices: It goes up to attract workers
It stays the same as every other job
check.why: Employers must pay extra to get enough people to do a hard or risky job.

lessons.title: Reading a Pay Stub
lessons.mainIdea: Gross pay is what you earn; net pay is what is left after taxes and deductions.
reading: Go back to Marcus. His *gross pay* was $480, the full amount he earned. Two lines on his stub are set by federal law. Social Security takes 6.2% of pay, and Medicare takes 1.45%. So 6.2% of $480 is $29.76, and 1.45% of $480 is $6.96.

Two other lines were income taxes. In this example, $15 went to federal income tax and $14 went to Illinois income tax. Money taken out of a paycheck is a *deduction*. Some workers also have deductions for health insurance or retirement savings.

Add the deductions: $29.76 + $6.96 + $15 + $14 = $65.72. Subtract from gross pay: $480 - $65.72 = $414.28. That is his *net pay*, the money that reaches his bank account. The big lesson: plan your spending with net pay, not gross pay.

words.d: the full amount you earn before anything is taken out
the amount you actually receive after taxes and other deductions
money taken out of a paycheck, such as taxes or insurance

look.title: Marcus's Pay Stub (example)
look.cite: Example pay stub; Social Security 6.2% and Medicare 1.45% are the employee tax rates set by federal law
look.prompt: What share of Marcus's gross pay did he take home? Round to the nearest whole percent.

check.q: Gross pay is $500 and deductions total $70. What is net pay?
check.why: Net pay = gross pay minus deductions: $500 - $70 = $430.

check.q: Social Security takes 6.2% of pay. How much is taken from $200?
Which number should you use to plan a budget?
choices: The largest number on the stub
check.why: Net pay is the money you really have to spend or save.

lessons.title: Needs, Wants and Trade-Offs
lessons.mainIdea: Every dollar can be spent only once, so a budget means choosing among needs and wants.
reading: Marcus has $414 from his check. He wants new sneakers for $120, a game for $60 and concert tickets for $90. He also must pay $40 a month for his phone and give $50 toward bus fare. These are example prices.

A *need* is something you must have to live or work, like food, housing, or a way to get to your job. A *want* is something nice to have but not required. Marcus's bus fare is a need because he rides the bus to work. The concert is a want.

Money is scarce, so each choice has an *opportunity cost*, the next-best thing you give up. If Marcus buys the sneakers, he may give up the concert. A common mistake is to call something a need just because you want it badly. Another is to list every item you skipped as the opportunity cost. It is only the next-best one.

words.d: something required to live or to work, like food, housing or transportation
something nice to have but not required
the next-best thing you give up when you make a choice

look.title: Marcus's List
look.text: After his phone and bus fare, Marcus has $324 left. The sneakers cost $120, the game $60 and the concert $90 (example prices). He also wants to save something.
look.prompt: If he buys all three, how much is left to save? Which one would you drop, and what is its opportunity cost?

check.q: Which is a need for a worker who rides the bus to work?
check.why: The bus gets the worker to the job, so fare is required.

check.q: Marcus picks sneakers over the concert. His next-best choice was the concert. What is his opportunity cost?
choices: The concert and the game and savings
check.why: Opportunity cost is only the next-best thing given up, not the item chosen or a list.

check.q: Marcus has $324. He buys items costing $120, $60 and $90. How much is left?

lessons.title: Building a Monthly Budget
lessons.mainIdea: A budget is a plan that lists income, then spending and saving, so money in covers money out.
reading: A *budget* is a plan for your money. Start with income. Then list what you expect to spend and save. The two sides should match. Let us build one for Ana, a young adult with $2,000 a month in net pay (an example).

Ana plans: rent $800, food $300, bus pass $75, phone $50, fun $250, clothes $125 and savings $400. Add them: $800 + $300 + $75 + $50 + $250 + $125 + $400 = $2,000. Every dollar has a job. Some expenses are fixed, the same each month, like rent. Others are variable, like food, which changes.

A budget works only if you track what really happens. Ana writes down what she spends for a month. She finds she spent $380 on food, not $300. So she cuts fun to $170 to stay even. If spending is more than income, a person runs short and may have to borrow.

words.d: a plan that shows expected income, spending and saving
a cost that stays the same each month, like rent
a cost that changes from month to month, like food

look.title: Ana's Monthly Budget (example)
look.cite: Made-up example budget for a $2,000 monthly net income
look.prompt: Which items are fixed expenses? What share of Ana's income goes to savings?

check.q: Ana spends $80 more on food than planned. What is one way to keep her budget balanced?
choices: Spend $80 less on something else, like fun
check.why: A budget balances when spending changes in one line are offset in another.

check.q: Which is a variable expense?
check.why: Grocery costs change each month. The others stay the same.

check.q: Income is $1,500. Planned spending and saving total $1,650. What is the problem?
choices: Planned spending is $150 more than income
check.why: $1,650 - $1,500 = $150 over. The plan spends money that is not there.

lessons.title: The 50/30/20 Idea
lessons.mainIdea: One simple guide splits net income into 50% needs, 30% wants and 20% savings.
reading: There is no single right budget. One popular guide is called 50/30/20. It is just one example of a starting point. It says about 50% of net income goes to needs, 30% to wants and 20% to savings or paying off debt.

Try it with $2,000 a month. 50% of $2,000 is $1,000 for needs. 30% is $600 for wants. 20% is $400 for savings. Check: $1,000 + $600 + $400 = $2,000. Try $1,200: $600 needs, $360 wants and $240 savings.

The guide may not fit everyone. In a city where rent is high, needs may take 60% or more. Then wants must shrink to keep savings. A common mistake is to treat 50/30/20 as a law. It is a tool to help you think about balance.

words.d: money set aside now to use later
the money you actually receive after taxes and deductions

look.title: Testing the Guide
look.text: Jordan's net pay is $3,000 a month. Rent, food, transport and insurance cost $1,800 (example amounts).
look.prompt: Using 50/30/20, how much should go to needs? Is Jordan above or below? What would you change?

check.q: Using 50/30/20, how much of $2,500 goes to savings?
Using 50/30/20, how much of $1,800 goes to wants?
A person's needs take 60% of income. To keep saving 20%, what must happen?
check.why: The parts must add to 100%: 60 + 20 + 20 = 100.

lessons.title: Saving Goals and Emergency Funds
lessons.mainIdea: Saving works best with a clear goal, and an emergency fund protects you from surprise costs.
reading: Tasha wants a $600 laptop. She can save $50 a week from her job. $600 divided by $50 is 12, so she will reach her goal in 12 weeks. A *saving goal* names what you want, how much it costs and when you want it.

Now picture a surprise. Tasha's bike breaks, and the repair costs $150. Without savings, she might borrow and pay extra. An *emergency fund* is money kept only for surprises like repairs, medical bills or losing a job. Many advisers suggest adults keep three to six months of expenses in one.

Savings goals can be short term, like a laptop in a few months. They can be long term, like college or a home years away. One helpful habit is to pay yourself first. Move savings out as soon as you are paid, before spending on wants.

words.d: money saved only for unexpected costs, like repairs or losing a job
a plan that names what you are saving for, how much and by when

look.title: Pay Yourself First
look.text: Leo earns $400 a month (example). He usually saves whatever is left at the end of the month, which is often nothing.
look.prompt: If Leo moves $60 into savings on payday, how much will he save in a year? Why might this work better?

check.q: A bike costs $300. You save $25 a week. How many weeks until you can buy it?
check.why: $300 divided by $25 = 12 weeks.

check.q: What is an emergency fund for?
choices: Surprise costs, like a car repair
check.why: An emergency fund covers costs you did not expect.

check.q: An adult's expenses are $2,000 a month. What would a three-month emergency fund hold?

lessons.title: Simple and Compound Interest
lessons.mainIdea: Simple interest is paid only on the starting amount; compound interest is also paid on interest already earned.
reading: When you keep money in a bank savings account, the bank pays you *interest*. Interest is a payment for letting someone use your money. The starting amount is called the *principal*. Say you put $100 in an account that pays 5% a year (an example rate).

With *simple interest*, you earn 5% of the $100, or $5, each year. After 3 years you have $100 + $5 + $5 + $5 = $115. The formula is principal times rate times years: $100 x 0.05 x 3 = $15 of interest.

With *compound interest*, you earn interest on your interest too. Year 1: $100 x 1.05 = $105. Year 2: $105 x 1.05 = $110.25. Year 3: $110.25 x 1.05 = $115.76. That is 76 cents more than simple interest. The gap is small at first, but it grows larger every year.

words.d: money paid for the use of money; savers earn it and borrowers pay it
the starting amount of money saved or borrowed
interest paid only on the principal
interest paid on the principal and on interest already earned

look.title: $100 at 5% a Year, Compounded (example)
look.cite: Made-up example: $100 at an example 5% yearly rate, compounded once a year
look.prompt: How much did the account grow in the first year? About how much in ten years?

check.q: You save $200 at 3% simple interest for 2 years. How much interest do you earn?
check.why: Simple interest = $200 x 0.03 x 2 = $12. $212 is the total, not the interest.

check.q: $100 earns 10% compound interest a year. How much is in the account after 2 years?
check.why: Year 1: $110. Year 2: $110 x 1.10 = $121. $120 would be simple interest.

check.q: Why does compound interest grow faster than simple interest?
choices: The bank adds a bonus every week
You earn interest on past interest
check.why: Each year's interest is added to the balance, so the next year's interest is figured on a bigger amount.

lessons.title: Why Starting Early Matters
lessons.mainIdea: Because of compounding, money saved early has more years to grow than money saved later.
reading: Meet two savers. Each uses an account paying 6% a year, an example rate. Maya puts in $1,000 at age 16. Sam waits and puts in $1,000 at age 28. Neither adds more money. Who ends up with more?

A shortcut called the *Rule of 72* estimates how long money takes to double. Divide 72 by the interest rate. 72 divided by 6 is 12, so money at 6% doubles about every 12 years. By age 28, Maya's $1,000 has become about $2,000, just as Sam starts.

By age 40, Sam's money has doubled once, to about $2,000. Maya's has doubled twice, to about $4,000. She saved the same amount, but she gave it more time. The key is time, not a big first deposit. A common mistake is to think small savings do not matter. Small amounts saved early can grow a lot.

words.d: interest paid on the principal and on interest already earned
a shortcut: divide 72 by the yearly interest rate to estimate the years it takes money to double

look.title: Two Savers
look.text: Maya saves $1,000 at 16. Sam saves $1,000 at 28. Both earn an example 6% a year and add nothing more.
look.prompt: Use the Rule of 72. How much does each have at 52? What did Maya's early start earn her?

check.q: Using the Rule of 72, about how long does money take to double at 8% a year?
check.why: 72 divided by 8 = 9 years.

check.q: Money doubles every 12 years. $500 is saved at 20. About how much is there at 44?
check.why: From 20 to 44 is 24 years, or two doublings: $500 to $1,000 to $2,000.

check.q: Why did Maya end with more than Sam, though both saved $1,000?
choices: Her money had more years to compound
check.why: Same amount, same rate. The only difference was time.

lessons.title: Where to Keep Your Savings
lessons.mainIdea: Banks and credit unions keep savings safe, and federal insurance protects deposits up to $250,000.
reading: Keeping cash in a shoe box earns no interest, and it can be lost or stolen. A *savings account* at a bank or credit union keeps money safe and pays interest. A *credit union* is a bank-like group owned by its members.

If a bank fails, deposits are protected. The FDIC insures bank deposits up to $250,000 per depositor, per bank, for each type of account. Credit unions have similar protection from a federal agency called the NCUA. So Marcus's $300 in savings is safe even if his bank has trouble.

Banks offer choices. A savings account lets you take money out easily. A *certificate of deposit*, or CD, often pays a higher rate. The catch is that you agree to leave the money there for a set time. The trade-off is easy access versus higher interest.

words.d: a bank account that keeps money safe and pays interest
a bank-like institution owned by its members
a deposit you leave in a bank for a set time, often for a higher interest rate

look.title: Adam Smith on Saving
look.text: Capitals are increased by parsimony, and diminished by prodigality and misconduct.
look.cite: Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations, Book II, Chapter 3, 1776
look.prompt: Parsimony means careful saving. Prodigality means wasteful spending. Put Smith's sentence into your own words.

check.q: What does FDIC insurance do?
choices: Protects bank deposits up to $250,000 if a bank fails
check.why: The FDIC insures deposits up to $250,000 per depositor, per bank, for each account type.

check.q: Why might someone choose a CD over a savings account?
choices: It often pays a higher rate
They can take money out any day with no penalty
check.why: CDs often pay more in exchange for leaving the money for a set time.

check.q: What is a downside of keeping savings in cash at home?
choices: It earns no interest and can be lost
It grows faster than a bank account
check.why: Cash at home does not grow and has no insurance.

review.q: Gross pay is $600. Deductions total $90. What is net pay?
You save $400 at 5% simple interest for 3 years. How much interest do you earn?

choices: A second pair of name-brand shoes
review.why: You can live and work without extra designer shoes.

review.q: Using 50/30/20, how much of $3,000 goes to needs?
$200 earns 10% compound interest a year. How much after 2 years?
Which pays you a set amount for a year of work?
review.why: A salary is a fixed yearly amount; a wage is paid per hour.

review.q: Why do many advisers suggest an emergency fund?
choices: To pay surprise costs without borrowing
To earn the highest possible return
review.why: An emergency fund is for the unexpected, so you do not need to borrow.

review.q: At 6% a year, about how long does it take money to double?
